overview: The Tuscarora were an influential people of the North Carolina Coastal Plain before many moved north after colonial warfare. They became the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and remain a living people. This imported outline is in central New York, so it misrepresents their homeland for the displayed 1492 to 1500 dates; it also is not their present reservation near Niagara Falls.

periods.title: North Carolina towns
periods.summary: River settlements sustained a powerful regional people with trading connections into Virginia.

periods.title: War, migration and confederacy
periods.summary: The colonial war drove migrations; Tuscarora joined the Haudenosaunee and later faced another war during the American Revolution.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: Tuscarora community life, institutions and language teaching continue beyond the map’s narrow date range.

items.text: Tuscarora towns did not all make the same choices as settlers expanded. In the early eighteenth century, Tom Blount’s Upper Towns maintained profitable colonial trade, while Hancock’s Lower Towns resisted growing pressure more directly. Treating every Tuscarora community as one military bloc hides these important political differences.

Nooherooka was built to shelter people under attack. Archaeological investigations found connected bunkers and tunnels with substantial stores of food and supplies. The fort occupied about one and a half acres behind high timber defenses. Protection required planning for families’ survival as well as positions for fighters.

Colonial troops and Native allies attacked Nooherooka in March 1713, burned the fort and killed or captured many defenders. Some survivors fled; others were enslaved. This disaster accelerated the dispersal of Tuscarora people and opened more of their homeland to colonial settlement.

The entire population did not leave North Carolina at once. A reservation established in 1717 in Bertie County served Blount’s people and became known as Indian Woods. It appears on eighteenth-century maps. The history of those who remained belongs alongside the better-known migration north.

In the early eighteenth century, Tuscarora joined the Haudenosaunee Confederacy as its sixth nation. During the American Revolution, many Tuscarora and Oneida supported the Americans as scouts and guides. Individual choices varied, and victory brought little compensation for the devastation Native communities had endured.

New York’s power project brought another struggle over land. In 1960, the United States Supreme Court permitted the taking of certain Tuscarora-owned lands for a Niagara hydroelectric reservoir, with compensation. The dispute concerned land the Nation had purchased; technological development imposed another loss on a community that had already rebuilt far from its southern homeland.

Excavation at Nooherooka began in 1990. The destruction layer offered researchers an unusually concentrated view of the fort’s final occupation. They compared buried evidence with a surviving battle map. The map records an attack from the attackers’ viewpoint, so archaeology provides another way to investigate what happened inside.

A Tuscarora cuff in the National Museum of the American Indian combines wool cloth, hide and glass beads. Raised beadwork gives decoration a three-dimensional surface. The museum bought it in 1937 through collector George Heye; that purchase dates its collection history, not necessarily the year someone sewed it.

Smithsonian photographs name Tuscarora women selling beadwork from outdoor tables at Niagara Falls, including Matilda Hill and her daughter Norma. These early-twentieth-century records connect beautiful objects with particular people and livelihoods. Family work and a busy visitor destination helped sustain a continuing artistic tradition.

A 2011 environmental-program profile describes saving Tuscarora White Corn and heirloom bean and squash seeds, then sharing them within the community. Its garden taught students growing techniques. Beans climbed corn stalks while squash spread over the ground: three useful crops shared the same patch rather efficiently.

That same 2011 profile records communal canning workshops where families brought produce to preserve together. A photograph shows a student learning to can deer meat with a pressure cooker. Food knowledge includes keeping the harvest usable after the garden stops producing, as well as growing it.

In 2019, Tuscarora collaborators and Cornell researcher Sam Bosco helped establish a school food forest with about thirty fruit and nut trees and shrubs. Earlier workshops had included tree identification and cooking with walnuts, acorns, chestnuts and hickories. A schoolyard could become a place to learn, harvest and eventually gather seeds for more trees.

sections.title: Words, memory and the living nation

items.text: In her 2013 field study, Paris Harper writes the Tuscarora self-name “Skaru:rȩɂ” and translates it as “People of the Shirt” or “People of the Hemp.” She connects it with the traditional use of dogbane, also called Indian hemp. This is an attested modern written form of a spoken name, not a fifteenth-century inscription.

The Nation’s current language program brings learners, teachers and advocates together to rebuild a Tuscarora-speaking community. Its official site also lists a school and a health center. Language, education and healthcare are parts of present community life, not just subjects preserved in historical collections.

For Nooherooka’s three-hundredth anniversary in 2013, Tuscarora delegates and East Carolina University prepared a memorial gathering and discussions of history, language and culture. Researchers also examined the old battle map with infrared imaging. Tuscarora families were central to remembering the site where their ancestors had suffered.

ending.text: The imported 1500 endpoint is not a Tuscarora ending. Colonial warfare caused deaths, enslavement and migration, followed by new alliances and communities. The Tuscarora Nation continues near Niagara Falls with community institutions and language revitalization.
